q: history and evolution of Impressionist art
a: Impressionism was a revolutionary art movement that emerged in France in the 1860s and flourished through the 1870s and 1880s. It marked a radical break from the academic painting conventions of the time. The movement began when a group of young artists including Claude Monet, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Edgar Degas, Camille Pissarro, Berthe Morisot, Alfred Sisley, and Frédéric Bazille began painting outdoors (en plein air) and capturing fleeting moments of light and atmosphere rather than carefully composed studio scenes. The term Impressionism originated from a derisive review of Monet's painting Impression, Sunrise (1872) at their first independent exhibition in 1874. The movement evolved through several phases: early Impressionism focused on landscapes and everyday life painted with visible brushstrokes and bright colors; middle Impressionism saw artists developing more individual styles; and post-Impressionism (1880s-1890s) included artists like Georges Seurat, Paul Cézanne, Vincent van Gogh, and Paul Gauguin who extended Impressionist ideas in new directions. Impressionist techniques included painting with small, visible brushstrokes, using pure colors rather than mixing on a palette, capturing the effects of natural light at different times of day, painting ordinary subject matter, and using unusual angles and cropped compositions influenced by photography and Japanese woodblock prints. The movement eventually spread beyond France to influence artists worldwide.
